name: Wand or fishing-rod toy
why: Best way to run the hunt → catch → eat sequence together.
how: Move it like prey: away from the cat, hiding behind furniture, then pausing.
Let the cat catch it at the end of every session.
Put the wand away afterwards so the string cannot be chewed.
safety: Supervised use only. Store string toys out of reach: swallowed string can cause serious intestinal injury.

name: Kicker or crinkle toy
why: Something to grab and bunny-kick, good for solo play.
how: Rotate a few toys each week to keep them interesting.
safety: Check for loose parts regularly and bin worn toys.

name: Cardboard box fort
why: Hiding and ambush spots lower stress and give climbing and scratching.
how: Pick a sturdy box with the flaps removed.
Cut two or three cat-sized openings, with edges smooth.
Place on its side, near where the family spends time.
Add a blanket inside if the cat likes it.
safety: Remove staples and tape. Avoid boxes that held chemicals.

name: Egg-carton foraging tray
why: Makes the cat work for food, which matches natural hunting.
how: Put a few dry biscuits in each cup.
Close it loosely and let the cat open it.
safety: Supervise the first few times and discard the carton once it is wet or shredded.

name: Toilet-roll treat tube
how: Fold the other end shut and roll it across the floor.
safety: Supervised use only. Do not use if the cat swallows cardboard.

name: Scrunched paper ball
why: A quiet chasing toy that costs nothing.
how: Scrunch a sheet of plain paper into a tight ball.
safety: Use plain paper only, no printed or coloured ink. Bin it when it is damp or chewed.
